analogy.p: Think of the Earth as a savings account holding a fixed amount of oil and ores (finite resources) that also earns a little interest every year (renewable resources like timber that regrow). Sustainable development is spending only the interest, or spending the savings so slowly and wisely that your grandchildren still have something left. Recycling is like paying some money back in. Phytomining and bioleaching are like finding a way to use the small coins left in the bottom of old pockets (low-grade ores). The analogy breaks down because you cannot pay oil back into the ground, and some damage, such as lost habitats, cannot be repaid at all.

bullets: **Warmth:** fuels such as natural gas, coal and oil are burned to heat homes and generate electricity, and wood and crops can be burned too.
**Shelter:** building materials such as limestone (for cement), clay (bricks), sand (glass), metals and timber all come from natural resources.
**Food:** produced by agriculture, which itself needs chemical help such as **fertilisers** and pesticides made in industry.
**Transport:** fuels (petrol, diesel, kerosene) come from crude oil, and vehicles are built from metals, plastics, glass and rubber.
**Clothing:** natural fibres (cotton, wool) come from agriculture, while synthetic fibres (polyesters, nylon) are made from crude oil.
The key exam idea: nearly every product you can name started life as a **raw material** extracted from the Earth, oceans or atmosphere.
core.h: Why humans use the Earth's resources
core.p: Humans depend on the **Earth's natural resources** for the basics of life: warmth, shelter, food and transport. A **resource** is any material or source of energy that people can use. Some come straight from nature (water, wood, wool, coal), while others are made by chemical processes from natural starting materials (plastics, medicines, fertilisers, metals). AQA expects you to understand that the whole chemical industry begins with raw materials taken from the Earth, the oceans and the atmosphere, and that using them wisely is a central problem for chemistry.

bullets: Agriculture supplies **food** (crops and animals), **timber** (for building, paper and fuel), **natural fibres** (cotton, wool, flax) and **crop-based fuels** such as ethanol.
Crops grow using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water (photosynthesis), so they are a **renewable** resource as long as they are replanted.
Fertilisers (containing nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium) replace the nutrients that crops remove from the soil.
Making fertilisers and pesticides needs raw materials and energy, which links agriculture to the finite resources used by industry.
Natural does not always mean sustainable: farming can destroy habitats, use large volumes of water and pollute rivers if run-off carries fertiliser into them.
You are not expected to know detailed farming methods, only that chemistry helps agriculture and that agriculture is a source of renewable resources.
core.p: **Natural resources**, supplemented by **agriculture**, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels. Farming allows us to produce much more food, wood and fibre than nature would give by itself, and it also supplies crops that can be turned into fuels. However, farming needs inputs such as land, water, energy and chemicals, so it too uses up resources. Chemistry plays an important role in improving agricultural processes, for example by making fertilisers that raise crop yields so that more people can be fed from the same area of land.

bullets: **Crude oil** is a mixture of hydrocarbons separated by fractional distillation into fuels and feedstocks for cracking and polymer production.
**Coal and natural gas:** natural gas (mostly methane) is also used to make hydrogen for the Haber process.
**Ores:** for example haematite (iron(III) oxide) for iron, bauxite (aluminium oxide) for aluminium, and copper-containing ores for copper.
**Limestone** (calcium carbonate) is used in construction and in the blast furnace, and is heated to make quicklime and (with clay) cement.
**Rock salt** gives sodium chloride, the raw material for the electrolysis of brine to make chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide.
Most of these materials took millions of years to form, so the Earth's supply is **finite** on human time-scales.
core.p: The Earth's crust is the source of most of the solid and fossil raw materials used by industry. **Fossil fuels** (crude oil, coal and natural gas) are used both as fuels and as **feedstocks** for the petrochemical industry, which makes plastics, solvents, detergents and medicines. **Metal ores** are rocks from which a metal can be extracted economically. **Limestone, clay, sand and rock salt** are quarried and used to make cement, bricks, glass and chemicals such as chlorine and sodium hydroxide.

bullets: **Oceans:** water, sodium chloride and other dissolved salts and minerals (for example magnesium and bromine compounds).
**Atmosphere:** about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and small amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases.
Liquid air is cooled until it condenses, then **fractionally distilled** because its gases have different boiling points.
Nitrogen from the air reacts with hydrogen to make **ammonia**, used to make fertilisers, so the atmosphere indirectly feeds the world.
Oxygen is used in steel making, in hospitals and in welding, and argon is used as an inert atmosphere.
Air and sea water are much more abundant than fossil fuels or ores, but turning them into useful products still needs **energy**.
core.h: Resources from the oceans and the atmosphere
core.p: The oceans and the atmosphere are also major sources of raw materials. Sea water contains large amounts of dissolved salts, especially sodium chloride, which can be obtained by evaporation and used to make other chemicals. The atmosphere is a mixture of gases; **nitrogen** and **oxygen** are separated from liquid air by fractional distillation, and nitrogen is the essential starting material for making ammonia in the Haber process, which in turn gives fertilisers. Water itself is a vital resource for drinking, agriculture and industry (and is the starting point for hydrogen in some processes).

bullets: **Finite examples:** crude oil, coal, natural gas, metal ores, limestone (in practice huge but not replaced).
**Renewable examples:** timber (if trees are replanted), crops, biofuels, wind, solar, hydroelectric and geothermal energy.
Wood is renewable only if new trees are planted as fast as old ones are cut down; felling a rainforest faster than it regrows is not sustainable.

A common error is to say that fossil fuels are 'non-renewable because they are not made any more'. The correct reasoning is that they **form far too slowly** (millions of years) to be replaced at the rate we use them.
Fossil fuels are used for energy AND as chemical feedstocks, so burning them wastes a raw material that is also needed to make plastics and medicines.
Recycling can turn a finite resource into a partly renewable one by keeping the material in use.
core.p: A **finite resource** is one that is used up faster than it is formed, so it will eventually run out. Crude oil, coal, natural gas and metal ores are finite because they take millions of years to form. A **renewable resource** is one that is replaced as fast as it is used, or that can be regrown or never runs out on a human time-scale, such as timber, crops, wind, solar and tidal energy. Whether a resource is called finite or renewable depends on the rate of use compared with the rate of replacement, not on whether it is natural.

bullets: **Depletion:** once crude oil or an ore is used up it cannot be replaced, so future generations cannot use it.
**Rising cost:** as high-grade ores are used, lower-grade ones must be processed, needing more energy, more equipment and more waste disposal.
**Habitat destruction:** quarrying, mining and drilling remove land and can pollute water and soil.
**Pollution and climate change:** burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas), sulfur dioxide and other pollutants.
**Waste:** large amounts of unwanted rock and spoil are produced when extracting metals from ores containing only a small percentage of metal.
These issues are why chemists search for new processes that use fewer resources, less energy and make less waste.
core.h: Why using finite resources is a problem
core.p: The main difficulty with finite resources is that supplies run out and the best, most easily extracted deposits are used first. As this happens, the remaining resources become harder and more expensive to obtain, and getting them often causes more environmental damage. Extracting and processing resources uses energy (often from burning fossil fuels), producing carbon dioxide, and mining destroys habitats and produces large amounts of waste rock. Using resources faster than they can be replaced therefore harms both the environment and the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

bullets: Memorise the definition: meets the needs of **current generations** without compromising the ability of **future generations** to meet **their own needs**.
It involves three linked ideas: protecting the **environment**, supporting the **economy** (jobs and costs) and meeting the needs of **people** (society).
Examples: using renewable energy, recycling metals, using catalysts to lower energy use, and replanting forests.
Sustainable does not mean 'never use anything': it means using resources at a rate and in a way that can be kept up.
Because needs and priorities differ, people may disagree about what is the most sustainable choice, so many questions ask you to **evaluate** options.
Sustainable development is the theme behind life cycle assessments, recycling and the choice between extracting metals by different methods.
core.p: **Sustainable development** is development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. This definition is worth learning word for word because it is directly examinable. It means we must balance people's need for food, energy, homes and goods today against protecting the environment and conserving resources for people in the future. Chemistry contributes by developing processes that are more efficient and less polluting, and by finding renewable alternatives to finite resources.

bullets: **Agriculture:** fertilisers (NPK) increase crop yields so less land is needed to feed people.
**Industry:** catalysts speed up reactions at lower temperatures and pressures, saving energy (for example in the Haber process).
**New products:** new materials such as polymers, alloys and composites replace scarcer materials or last longer.
**Cleaner processes:** removing pollutants from waste gases and treating waste water before release.
**Alternative extraction:** developing methods such as phytomining and bioleaching so that low-grade ores can still be used (Higher tier).
**Energy:** developing fuels and technologies that use renewable resources instead of finite ones.
core.h: The role of chemistry in improving processes
core.p: Chemistry plays an important role in improving agricultural and industrial processes to provide new products, and in sustainable development. Chemists work to make industrial processes more efficient and less wasteful, and to develop new materials that last longer or can be recycled. Better processes give the same product while using less raw material and energy and making less waste or pollution, which makes them both greener and cheaper. This is why chemical industry decisions are judged on cost, energy, raw materials, yield and environmental impact together.

bullets: **Reduce:** use less material, for example lighter packaging or longer-lasting products.
**Reuse:** use an item again without reprocessing, such as refilling glass bottles.
**Recycle:** collect and reprocess waste into new materials, saving raw materials and often a large amount of energy (see the recycling note).
Use **renewable energy** (wind, solar, hydroelectric) in place of fossil fuels to cut carbon dioxide emissions.
Improve **efficiency:** higher yields, catalysts, and recycling of heat and unreacted materials so less is wasted.
Use **renewable feedstocks**, such as crop-based materials, in place of crude oil where possible.
core.p: There are several practical ways to make the use of resources more sustainable. The usual strategy is summarised as reduce, reuse and recycle, supported by developing renewable energy and more efficient processes. Each approach reduces the amount of new raw material that has to be extracted, cuts the energy used and reduces the amount of waste sent to landfill. These ideas are explored more fully in the topics on recycling and life cycle assessments, but you should be able to give clear, specific examples here.

bullets: Quote figures from the data (with units) rather than just saying 'it uses less'.
Compare like with like: energy per kilogram of product, or waste per tonne of metal.
Consider the whole process, not just one stage: a 'green' material may need a lot of energy to make.
Mention both short-term and long-term effects, and effects on both people and the environment.
End with a justified conclusion; a mark is often given for a reasoned judgement, not just a list.
Link back to the definition of sustainable development in your explanation.
core.p: Examiners often give a table, graph or short passage and ask you to evaluate whether a process or product is sustainable. A good answer uses the data, makes a clear judgement and supports it with reasons that link to sustainable development: the resources used, the energy needed, the waste and pollution produced, and the cost. Remember that data on energy and waste are objective, while deciding which environmental impact matters most is a value judgement. Always give both an advantage and a disadvantage before reaching a conclusion if the question asks you to evaluate.

bullets: A **low-grade ore** contains a small proportion of the metal; for example, an ore with 1% copper needs about 100 tonnes of ore to yield 1 tonne of copper.
Traditional mining involves digging up, transporting and crushing rock, then smelting or electrolysis, all using energy and producing waste rock.
Both methods named in the spec, **phytomining** and **bioleaching**, are used mainly for **copper** in AQA questions.
They avoid some of the damage caused by large-scale mining and use less energy than smelting.
They allow metal to be obtained from ores and waste that would not be worth mining by traditional methods.
Both methods are slower than traditional extraction; this is the main disadvantage examiners look for.
core.h: Higher tier: why we need alternative ways of extracting metals
core.p: The supply of high-grade metal ores (rich in the metal) is limited, because the richest deposits have already been mined. We therefore now have to process **low-grade ores**, which contain only a small percentage of the metal. Using traditional mining and extraction on these ores needs huge quantities of rock to be dug up, crushed and heated or electrolysed, which uses a lot of energy and leaves enormous amounts of waste. New ways of extracting metals from low-grade ores and from waste, such as phytomining and bioleaching, are being developed to reduce this environmental impact and conserve the remaining high-grade ores.

bullets: Step 1: **grow plants** on soil that contains low levels of the metal (for example copper compounds).
Step 2: the plants **absorb the metal compounds** through their roots and concentrate them in their leaves and stems.
Step 3: **harvest** the plants and **dry** them.
Step 4: **burn** the plants; the **ash** contains the metal compounds (for example copper compounds).
Step 5: dissolve the ash in sulfuric acid to make a **solution of copper sulfate**, then extract copper by **electrolysis** or by **displacement using scrap iron**.
Displacement: iron is more reactive than copper, so Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu.
At the cathode in electrolysis, copper ions gain electrons: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (reduction).
**Disadvantage:** very slow, because plants take months or years to grow, and it needs land.
core.p: **Phytomining** uses plants to absorb metal compounds through their roots as they grow, concentrating the metal in the plant tissue. The plants are then harvested, dried and burned, and the metal compounds are left in the ash. The metal (for example copper) is then extracted from the ash. Phytomining is suited to low-grade ores and to soil contaminated by mining waste, and it avoids having to dig up and process huge quantities of rock.

bullets: Bacteria are added to a heap or tank of low-grade ore (and air and water are supplied).
The bacteria gain energy from the ore and produce a **leachate solution** containing the metal ions (copper ions, Cu2+).
The leachate is collected and the metal is extracted by **displacement with scrap iron** or by **electrolysis**.
Displacement uses a more reactive metal: iron displaces copper from copper sulfate solution as copper is below iron in the reactivity series.
Bioleaching works on low-grade ores that would not be economic to smelt, and it uses much less energy than smelting.
**Disadvantages:** slow, and the leachate (often acidic) can contain toxic metal compounds and must be contained so it does not pollute rivers and groundwater.
core.p: **Bioleaching** uses bacteria to extract metals from low-grade ores. The bacteria feed on the ore, breaking it down and producing a solution called a **leachate** that contains metal compounds (for example copper ions). The metal is then extracted from the leachate. Because the bacteria do much of the work, bioleaching avoids the need to heat the ore at high temperatures or to dig up and dump huge amounts of rock, so it is less harmful to the environment than traditional mining.

bullets: **Traditional mining:** fast, large output, needs high-grade ore, high energy, large waste, destroys habitats.
**Phytomining:** low energy, uses low-grade soils and waste, very slow, needs land and time, burning plants releases carbon dioxide.
**Bioleaching:** low energy, uses low-grade ores, slow, risk of toxic leachate if not contained.
All three produce a solution or compound that must then be reduced or displaced to obtain the metal.
In an exam evaluate by giving one advantage and one disadvantage of each, then a conclusion that links to sustainable development.
Do not claim that either new method has 'no environmental impact'; they simply reduce it.
core.p: For an evaluation you should compare phytomining, bioleaching and traditional mining on the same criteria. Traditional mining and smelting is fast and gives large amounts of metal, but it needs high-grade ores, uses large amounts of energy and produces large amounts of waste rock and carbon dioxide. Phytomining and bioleaching can use low-grade ores and waste with less energy and less habitat destruction, but they are much slower and give smaller amounts of metal at a time. Which is best depends on the priorities: speed and quantity or environmental impact and conservation of resources.

bullets: **Extraction of metals (4.4):** reduction with carbon, electrolysis, reactivity series; Higher tier displacement reactions used in phytomining and bioleaching.
**Crude oil and fuels (4.7):** fractional distillation, cracking and polymers show oil as both fuel and feedstock.
**Atmosphere (4.9):** burning fuels releases carbon dioxide and pollutants; carbon footprint ideas.
**Life cycle assessments and recycling (4.10):** judging products across their whole life, and reusing materials.
**Haber process and NPK fertilisers (4.10):** nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from natural gas make ammonia for fertilisers.
**Potable water (4.10):** water is a resource that must be treated before use and again before release.
core.p: Sustainable use of resources is a unifying theme in the specification, so it connects to many other topics. You should be able to draw on these links when a question asks you to explain why a process matters or to evaluate a process in context. Making these links also makes it easier to remember facts because you understand the reasoning behind them rather than learning each topic in isolation.

exam: State the definition of sustainable development in full: 'meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs' (usually 1-2 marks).
'Give one reason' questions (1 mark): crude oil is finite / takes millions of years to form / will run out.
'Describe' questions on phytomining (up to 4 marks): grow plants, they absorb copper compounds, harvest and burn, ash contains copper compounds, extract copper by electrolysis or displacement.
'Describe' bioleaching (3-4 marks): bacteria, low-grade ore, produce leachate containing copper ions, extract the copper by electrolysis or displacement with scrap iron.
'Explain why' extraction is needed from low-grade ores: high-grade ores are running out, so low-grade ores must be used.
'Evaluate' (4-6 marks): give advantages and disadvantages of each method, use data from the question, and end with a justified conclusion.
Always use the exact words 'finite', 'renewable', 'low-grade ore', 'leachate' and 'ash' when the question allows; these earn marks.
For displacement, give the reason: iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulfate solution.
Write balanced equations with state symbols if asked: Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) → FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s).
Graph or table questions: read values carefully, quote numbers with units, and describe the trend before explaining it.
Do not refer to 'pollution' vaguely; say what pollutant (carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, toxic leachate) and what harm it causes.

mistakes.r: Finite resources form so slowly (millions of years) that they are used up faster than they are replaced.
mistakes.w: Finite resources are 'not made any more'.

mistakes.r: Sustainable development meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
mistakes.w: Sustainable means we never use anything up.

mistakes.r: Renewable resources still need land, water and energy, and can be harmful if overused (for example cutting down forests faster than they regrow).
mistakes.w: Renewable resources have no environmental impact.

mistakes.r: Phytomining uses plants; bioleaching uses bacteria. Do not mix them up.
Burning the plants leaves ash containing copper compounds; the copper is then extracted from a solution made from the ash by electrolysis or displacement.
mistakes.w: Plants are burned to get the copper out as pure copper.

mistakes.r: Bioleaching and phytomining are slow; their advantages are lower energy use and the ability to use low-grade ores with less environmental damage.
mistakes.w: Bioleaching is the best because it is fast and cheap.

mistakes.r: Low-grade ores contain only a small percentage of metal; they are now needed because high-grade ores are running out.
mistakes.w: Low-grade ores are not used because they are useless.

mistakes.r: Crude oil is also a feedstock for plastics and chemicals, so burning it wastes a raw material.

summary: You need to know that the Earth, oceans and atmosphere supply the finite and renewable resources used for warmth, shelter, food and transport, define sustainable development, explain how chemistry improves agricultural and industrial processes, and (Higher tier) describe phytomining and bioleaching as ways of extracting metals from low-grade ores. It matters because examiners use this topic to test whether you can evaluate processes in terms of resources, energy, waste and the needs of future generations.

terms.d: A material or source of energy found in nature that can be used by humans, such as crude oil, ores, water, timber and air.
A resource that is used up faster than it can be replaced, so it will eventually run out (for example crude oil, coal and metal ores).
A resource that is replaced as fast as it is used or can be regrown, such as timber, crops, wind and solar energy.
Development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
A natural material taken from the Earth, oceans or atmosphere that is processed to make a product.
A raw material used as the starting point for the chemical industry, for example crude oil used to make plastics.
Farming to produce food, timber, fibres and crops used as fuels.
A rock that contains enough of a metal or metal compound to make it economic to extract the metal.
An ore containing a large percentage of the metal compound, so extraction is easier and cheaper.
An ore containing only a small percentage of the metal, which is expensive and wasteful to extract by traditional methods.
Using plants to absorb metal compounds from the soil; the plants are burned and the metal is extracted from the ash (Higher tier).
Using bacteria to produce a leachate solution containing metal compounds from low-grade ores (Higher tier).
The solution containing dissolved metal compounds produced when bacteria break down an ore in bioleaching.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound, for example iron displacing copper from copper sulfate.
Using an electric current to decompose an ionic compound in solution or molten form, with metal formed at the cathode.
Collecting and reprocessing waste materials into new products so that fewer new raw materials are needed.

worked.ans: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
worked.q: State what is meant by sustainable development. (2 marks)
steps: Recall the definition word for word.
Include the idea of meeting their own needs.

worked.ans: Plants are grown on soil containing low levels of copper compounds and absorb them through their roots. The plants are harvested, dried and burned to leave ash that contains copper compounds. The ash is dissolved in sulfuric acid to make copper sulfate solution, and copper is obtained by electrolysis or by displacement using scrap iron (iron is more reactive than copper).
worked.q: Describe how phytomining can be used to obtain copper from a low-grade ore or contaminated soil. (4 marks)
steps: Grow plants on the soil containing copper compounds.
The plants absorb the copper compounds through their roots.
Harvest, dry and burn the plants.
The ash contains the copper compounds; dissolve it in sulfuric acid and extract copper by electrolysis or by displacement with scrap iron.

worked.ans: 250 tonnes of ore (about 248 tonnes of it becomes waste rock).
worked.q: A low-grade ore contains 0.80% copper by mass. Calculate the mass of ore that must be processed to obtain 2.0 tonnes of copper, assuming all the copper is extracted. (3 marks)
steps: Mass of ore = mass of copper ÷ fraction of copper = 2.0 ÷ 0.0080.
Check: 0.0080 × 250 = 2.0 tonnes. Waste rock is about 250 - 2.0 = 248 tonnes.
